# Arms control and disarmament agreements (`arms_control`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: helped by security_dilemma_arms_race, international_law_sovereignty, game_theory, military_intelligence_codebreaking, deterrence
- Core idea: Rivals can both gain by agreeing to limit the number, type or placing of weapons, because an unlimited race leaves both poorer and no safer. An agreement holds only if each side can check that the other complies (inspection, observers, counting what is easy to count such as large ships or fortresses) and if cheating would be detected in time to respond. The purpose is not friendship but stability: fewer reasons to strike first, less money wasted, and lines of contact that work in a crisis.
- Pitfalls:
  - Treating verification as a guarantee of compliance, or assuming an agreement without formal inspections must fail
  - Limiting one category shifts the race into the next (cruiser competition after the 1922 treaty, which also limited aircraft-carrier tonnage)
  - Bans proclaimed by an authority without means of enforcement are ignored (crossbow ban of 1139)
  - Disarmament imposed on the defeated breeds evasion and revenge (Carthage, Germany after 1919)
  - A weapon that offers a decisive advantage is almost never given up; bans succeed with weapons of doubtful usefulness
- History: china: 546 BC – conference of the Spring and Autumn states agrees to cease war, held for some years; rome: 201 BC – peace treaty limits Carthage to ten warships and no war elephants; 188 BC – similar terms for the Seleucid kingdom at Apamea; europe: 989–1040s – Peace and Truce of God restrict when and against whom knights may fight; 1139 – Second Lateran Council bans crossbows and bows against Christians, without effect; 1868 – St Petersburg Declaration; 1899 and 1907 – Hague conferences; east_asia: 1588 – Hideyoshi's sword hunt disarms the Japanese peasantry (internal arms control); americas: 1817 – Rush-Bagot agreement limits armed vessels on the Great Lakes, allowing a small patrol force; global: 1922 – Washington Naval Treaty fixes battleship ratios; 1925 – Geneva gas protocol; 1963 – partial nuclear test ban; 1968 – Non-Proliferation Treaty; 1972 – SALT I and ABM Treaty
- Read:
  - Thomas C. Schelling & Morton H. Halperin, Strategy and Arms Control (1961)
  - Hedley Bull, The Control of the Arms Race (1961)
  - Polybius, Histories XV.18
